chapter: Favorite bands, advice and family reflections
title: Glasses, age and reluctance about bop
summary: At 66 he does not expect to play as before; his son says inactivity came from reluctance about changes in jazz.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: When I asked him what some of the things he was interested in doing with the money being paid him for these interviews, he said he would like to get some new eye glasses and his teeth fixed teaching. Perhaps would that make you feel like playing some more ...
I can play just as good with these as I can without them (?) get some new ones because I know I need them and I know it.
You can't do today what you did when you were six years old.
And ain't going to try either.
I'm 66 and why should I play as good today.

In all honesty I want to kind of add this little point some of the inactivity in the past 15 to 20 years I've spent has been a kind of reluctance to accept the change that has taken place in jazz music. I mean the transition from swing and the dixie land and nee-bop and hard top style to bop ... that has been a large part of the inactivity and I think ...
That is because of our thing of being now oriented or some people call it some form of survival that we don't accommodate our own.
Oh, we definitely don't. No doubt about it.

... Peewee Russell or Benny Goodman or other guys sitting on Park Avenue, I feel that every-thing that Jack Teagarden got, he should have got double That's exactly how I feel about it. You know the system we are black in the white land so that says it all as far as what we've got and what we have not got and all of the things that have happened to us because it's happened to every one of us.
